analysis.one_liner: Exempts livestock manure from Superfund hazardous-waste liability and from emergency toxic-release reporting.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 192 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote; it died in subcommittee when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the Superfund law so that livestock manure — defined broadly to include animal waste, digestive emissions like ammonia, process water, and related byproducts — could never be treated as a hazardous substance or pollutant. It would also have exempted manure-related releases from the emergency notification requirements of the community right-to-know law, meaning large feedlots would no longer have to report significant releases of gases like ammonia and hydrogen sulfide. The practical effect would be to shield large livestock operations from cleanup liability and reporting duties that currently exist under federal environmental law. The bill never advanced past subcommittee referral and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been large livestock operations — the big poultry, hog, and dairy feeding operations whose waste and air emissions would be permanently shielded from Superfund cleanup liability and from emergency-release reporting. Smaller family farms would also have gained certainty that everyday manure use could never trigger federal hazardous-waste law, which was the sponsors' stated rationale.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large livestock and poultry feeding operations

how_it_helps.text: It removes manure from the definitions of 'hazardous substance' and 'pollutant or contaminant' under CERCLA, eliminating the possibility that farms could be held responsible for cleaning up sites under the Superfund law because of manure.

It exempts manure-related releases from the emergency notification requirements of SARA, so livestock operations would no longer have to report releases of manure-associated emissions such as ammonia and hydrogen sulfide.
It wipes out any paperwork obligations for manure under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act, reducing compliance costs for livestock operators.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the costs would have fallen on people living near large feedlots, who would lose the current requirement that significant releases of manure-related gases be reported to them, and potentially on taxpayers, who can end up covering cleanup costs when the parties responsible for a contaminated site are shielded from liability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rural residents near large feedlots, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The emergency-notification exemption would end the requirement that large livestock operations report significant releases of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide, removing the information neighbors of big feedlots currently receive under the community right-to-know law.

The definition of manure is sweeping — it covers not just animal waste but digestive emissions, process water, bedding, compost, and any byproducts or constituents originating from them — so it would shield air emissions and waste streams from very large operations, not just routine farm manure.

If a site contaminated by livestock waste ever needed cleanup, blocking the designation of manure as a hazardous substance would make it harder to compel the companies responsible to pay, shifting costs toward the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper, sparing ordinary farm manure from hazardous-waste law is reasonable — manure spread on fields was never a realistic cleanup target. But the bill's definition reached far beyond that, covering emissions, process water, and byproducts from the largest feedlots, and it would have removed the community's right to know about large releases of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide while shifting any cleanup costs at contaminated sites from the industry that created them to the public. The death of the bill preserved the legal uncertainty its sponsors cited, but it also preserved cleanup accountability and release notification for people living near big operations. On balance the bill's drawbacks outweighed its stated benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees and never came back — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ralph Hall introduced the bill on November 16, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

Within the following weeks it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials, and no further committee action was ever recorded.
It accumulated 192 cosponsors, including 157 Republicans and 35 Democrats, but never received a committee vote or reached the House floor.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: people living near large feedlots keep their community right-to-know notification of major manure-related gas releases, and the industry remains subject to existing Superfund law. The livestock industry, despite its broad support in the House, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Neighbors of large feedlots; status quo held

for.name: Rep. Ralph M. Hall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 157 House Republicans and 35 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill 192 names and bipartisan backing, though it never reached a vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and referred it to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials; the committee never held a markup or reported the bill out.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment; no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily Republican but genuinely bipartisan: of the 192 cosponsors, 157 were Republicans and 35 were Democrats, including members from farm states in both parties.

industries.industry: Large livestock operations (concentrated animal feeding operations — poultry, hog, and dairy)
industries.note: The bill would free large feedlots from any Superfund cleanup liability tied to manure and from emergency-release reporting for manure-associated emissions like ammonia and hydrogen sulfide, cutting compliance costs and legal exposure. For ordinary people, it means less information about large releases of livestock gases near their homes and a greater chance that cleanup costs at contaminated sites fall to the public. The bill died, so none of this took effect.
